To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) WTP for ACT was less than the real price of ACT; (2) the decision taken in Tanzania by the Ministry of Health and Social Welfare to subsidize ACT at a consumer price level of US$ 0.3–0.4 at governmental health care centres and at US$ 0,28–0.4 through the ADDO programme appears well founded; (3) a subsidy is needed to make ACT affordable and accessible for all, and (4) the

WTP for a course of ACT for children in rural Tanzania was less than its cost and a subsidy was needed to ensure its affordability; WTP for ACT was not affected by socio-economic status; the median annual cost for non-subsidised ACT in an average household in this study was calculated as US $ 6.0; the cost of non-subisidized ACT represented only 0.9 % of the average total annual consumption expenditures as estimated for the whole population; and
WTP and ATP for ACT are lower than its real price and that WTP and ability to pay are not associated with socio-economic status.
